name: Leg raise
angleNote: Hip flexion: 0° = legs in line with the trunk, 90° = legs at a right angle to it. Hip at the origin.

segments.massNote: Both legs: segment mass as a fraction of body mass (twice one leg), and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The lower legs include the feet (combined centre of mass along knee → ankle; the foot's own position is approximated).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Hip→knee and knee→ankle in metres, typical adult.

strengthCurve.label: Hip flexor strength (both hips)
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric hip-flexion torque vs hip flexion, strongest with the hip straight or slightly extended (peak at −12°), measured standing with the knee slightly bent (tested −29° to 74°; further hip flexion is held flat at the 74° value, which is extrapolation: the hip flexors are short there and likely weaker still). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3 (hip flexion: C2 0.738, C3 −0.214 rad). Peak torque default: twice the same table's C1 for young men (both hips; 0.113 × body weight × height = 142 Nm each at 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strengthCurve.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

muscles.name: Iliopsoas (hip flexors)
muscles.note: The main hip flexor: the psoas from the lumbar spine and the iliacus from the pelvis, both to the thigh. It lifts the legs; the abdominals don't, they hold the pelvis. Fine-wire EMG: the iliacus worked harder in straight-leg lifts than in sit-ups, and two-leg lifts also needed the abdominals (Andersson et al.).
muscles.source: Andersson EA, Nilsson J, Ma Z, Thorstensson A (1997). Abdominal and hip flexor muscle activation during various training exercises. Eur J Appl Physiol 75(2):115–123. doi:10.1007/s004210050135 (6 men, fine-wire EMG of the iliacus)

muscles.name: Rectus femoris (quadriceps)
muscles.note: The one quadriceps head that crosses the hip. In the hanging knee-up it reached only 15% of its maximum (Escamilla et al.), while the abdominals worked hard; with the knees bent it is short at the hip and slack at the knee. Higher with straight legs (not measured).
muscles.source: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, Jew P, Kelleher P, Burnham T, Busch J, D'Anna K, Mowbray R, Imamura RT (2006). Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Phys Ther 86(5):656–671. doi:10.1093/ptj/86.5.656 (Table 2: % of maximal isometric activation, 21 adults)

muscles.name: Rectus abdominis
muscles.note: The hip flexors pull the pelvis forward (arching the lower back) as hard as they lift the legs; the abdominals hold it, and at the top curl the pelvis up. In the hanging knee-up (with straps) the rectus abdominis reached 69–75% of its maximum (upper and lower part; Escamilla et al.), as high as in any exercise they tested.
muscles.source: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, Jew P, Kelleher P, Burnham T, Busch J, D'Anna K, Mowbray R, Imamura RT (2006). Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Phys Ther 86(5):656–671. doi:10.1093/ptj/86.5.656 (Table 2: % of maximal isometric activation, 21 adults)

muscles.name: External oblique
muscles.note: Braces the trunk with the rectus abdominis and stops the body swinging: 79% of its maximum in the hanging knee-up (internal oblique 85%; Escamilla et al.).
muscles.source: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, Jew P, Kelleher P, Burnham T, Busch J, D'Anna K, Mowbray R, Imamura RT (2006). Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Phys Ther 86(5):656–671. doi:10.1093/ptj/86.5.656 (Table 2: % of maximal isometric activation, 21 adults)

phases.name: Start
phases.text: Legs in line with the trunk: the hip flexors are long and strongest. Lying down, this is where the legs' weight has its longest lever.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Lever and strength cross over: lying, the load falls; hanging, it rises.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Hanging, the legs are horizontal at 90°: the longest lever while the hip flexors are short and weak. The hardest point, and the reason many swing or bend the knees.

variants.name: Hanging leg raise
variants.notes: Hanging from a bar, straight legs. Torque grows with the sine of the hip angle: nothing at the bottom, most with the legs horizontal.

variants.name: Hanging knee raise
variants.notes: Knees bent 90°: with the thighs horizontal the lower legs hang straight below the knees, closer to the hip: about a quarter less torque than straight legs. The thighs' weight stays the same.

variants.name: Lying leg raise
variants.notes: On the back, straight legs. The hardest point is the start, just off the floor, where the legs are horizontal; at 90° they are vertical and weigh nothing on the hips.

placement.label: Knee bend
placement.hint: 0° = legs straight. Bending the knees brings the lower legs' weight (and an ankle weight) closer to the hip: a shorter lever, so a lighter lift.

trunk3d.note: 3D view: the trunk muscles of the OpenSim lumbar spine model (Christophy et al. 2012, MIT licence), shaded by this exercise's muscle effort. Groups the exercise doesn't load stay grey. Set on the body as it lies or hangs; the legs move, the trunk stays straight.
